{{Short description|Variance of random sum}}

The '''Blackwell-Girshick equation''' is an equation in [[probability theory]] that allows for the calculation of the [[variance]] of random sums of [[random variable]]s.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Blackwell|first1=D. A.|last2=Girshick|first2=M. A.|title=Theory of games and statistical decisions|publisher=Courier Corporation|year=1979}}</ref> It is the equivalent of [[Wald's lemma]] for the expectation of composite distributions.

It is named after [[David Blackwell]] and [[Meyer Abraham Girshick]].
== Statement ==
Let <math> N </math> be a random variable with values in <math> \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} </math>, let <math> X_1, X_2, X_3, \dots</math> be [[independent and identically distributed]] random variables, which are also independent of <math>N</math>, and assume that the second [[moment (statistics)|moment]] exists for all <math>X_i</math> and <math>N</math>. Then, the random variable defined by
:<math>Y:=\sum_{i=1}^NX_i</math>
has the variance
:<math>\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\operatorname{Var}(N)\operatorname{E}(X_1)^2+\operatorname{E}(N)\operatorname{Var}(X_1)</math>.

The Blackwell-Girshick equation can be derived using [[conditional variance]] and variance decomposition.
If the <math> X_i </math> are natural number-valued random variables, the derivation can be done elementarily using the [[chain rule]] and the [[probability-generating function]].<ref>{{citation|page=109|author=Achim Klenke|date=2013|doi=10.1007/978-3-642-36018-3|edition=3rd|isbn=978-3-642-36017-6|location=Berlin Heidelberg|publisher=Springer-Verlag|title=Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie|s2cid=242882110 }}</ref>

== Proof ==
For each <math>n\ge 0</math>, let <math>\chi_n</math> be the random variable which is 1 if <math>N</math> equals <math>n</math> and 0 otherwise, and let <math>Y_n:=X_1+\cdots+X_n</math>.  Then
:<math>\begin{align} \operatorname{E}(Y^2) 
& = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \operatorname{E}(\chi_n Y_n^2)\\
&=  \sum_{n=0}^\infty \operatorname{P}(N=n) \operatorname{E}(Y_n^2)\\
&=  \sum_{n=0}^\infty\operatorname{P}(N=n) (\operatorname{Var}(Y_n)+\operatorname{E}(Y_n)^2)\\
&=  \sum_{n=0}^\infty\operatorname{P}(N=n) (n \operatorname{Var}(X_1)+n^2\operatorname{E}(X_1)^2)\\
&= \operatorname{E}(N) \operatorname{Var}(X_1) + \operatorname{E}(N^2) \operatorname{E}(X_1)^2.
\end{align}</math>
By [[Wald's equation]], under the given hypotheses, <math>\operatorname{E}(Y)=\operatorname{E}(N) \operatorname{E}(X_1)</math>.  Therefore,
:<math>\begin{align} \operatorname{Var}(Y)&=\operatorname{E}(Y^2)-\operatorname{E}(Y)^2\\
&= \operatorname{E}(N) \operatorname{Var}(X_1) + \operatorname{E}(N^2) \operatorname{E}(X_1)^2 - \operatorname{E}(N)^2 \operatorname{E}(X_1)^2 \\
&= \operatorname{E}(N) \operatorname{Var}(X_1) + \operatorname{Var}(N) \operatorname{E}(X_1)^2,
\end{align}</math>
as desired.{{r|K2014|at=§5.1, Theorem 5.10}}

== Example ==
Let <math> N </math> have a [[Poisson distribution]] with expectation <math> \lambda </math>, and let <math>X_1, X_2, \dots</math> follow a [[Bernoulli distribution]] with parameter <math> p </math>.  In this case, <math>Y</math> is also Poisson distributed with expectation <math>\lambda p</math>, so its variance must be <math>\lambda p</math>.  We can check this with the Blackwell-Girshick equation: <math>N</math> has variance <math>\lambda</math> while each <math>X_i</math> has mean <math>p</math> and variance <math>p(1-p)</math>, so we must have
:<math> \operatorname{Var}(Y)= \lambda p^2+\lambda p (1-p) = \lambda p </math>.

== Application and related concepts ==
The Blackwell-Girshick equation is used in [[actuarial mathematics]] to calculate the variance of composite distributions, such as the [[compound Poisson distribution]]. [[Wald's equation]] provides similar statements about the expectation of composite distributions.
